title: Sherpa Tensing — Camp Seven: Future Simple (will) (A2)

hero.h1: The weather you can't see yet
hero.lede: Camp five was the route you'd already chosen. Camp seven is everything you haven't: the decision you make in the moment, the offer, the promise, and the prediction you can't point at any evidence for. Will is the future you believe in rather than the future you can see.

cards.head: A decision made as you speak
cards.body: You didn't plan it. You are deciding now, out loud.

cards.head: An offer
cards.body: Volunteering to do something for someone.

cards.head: A promise
cards.body: Committing yourself, often with a time.

cards.head: A prediction or belief
cards.body: What you think will happen, with no evidence to point at.

cards.head: A refusal
cards.body: Won't is the strongest way to say no — even about objects.

cards.head: A future fact
cards.body: Something certain that nobody chose and nobody can change.

cards.head: Wh- questions
cards.body: question word + will + subject + base verb?

charts.head: Conjugation chart
charts.note: Will is a modal verb, and modals do not change for person — no -s, ever. The verb after it is always the bare infinitive.

charts.head: Shall — the one place it still lives
charts.note: In modern English shall has almost vanished, except in questions with I and we, where it offers or suggests.

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Nearly every error with will is one of these.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: When I will arrive, I'll call.
After when, if, as soon as and until, use the present.

charts.note: Camp five and camp seven stand on the same square of the timeline. The question is never when — it is when the decision was made and what the prediction rests on.

head: Situation
Will
Going to
rows:
Spontaneous — made as you speak.
"Fine — I'll do it myself."

Made before you spoke.
"I'm going to hand in my notice."

Opinion, belief, guess.
"I think it'll rain later."

Evidence you can point at.
"Look at those clouds — it's going to rain."

The natural choice.
"I'll help you move."

charts.example: Both are correct far more often than teachers admit. The test is whether the sentence would still be true if you had said nothing.

sections.label: Trail markers
sections.title: Signal words

signals.head: Future time markers
items: in a moment / in an hour

signals.head: Opinion and belief cues
items: I expect / I suppose / I hope

sections.example: The opinion cues are the real giveaway: I think, I'm sure and probably almost always take will, because what follows is a belief and not a plan.

diagram.intro: The same line as camp five, in a different colour. Will stands in exactly the same place on it as going to — which is the point: the timeline cannot tell them apart, only the reason behind the sentence can. Click each block to name it and see it in a sentence.

quiz.prompt: "The phone's ringing." "Don't get up — I _____ answer it."
quiz.hint: You are deciding at this second.
quiz.explain: A decision taken at the moment of speaking takes will. Going to would mean you had planned to answer that call before it rang.

quiz.prompt: That bag looks heavy. _____ I carry it for you?
quiz.explain: Offers with I and we take shall in questions: Shall I carry it? "Will I carry it?" asks about the future, not about helping.

quiz.prompt: I promise I _____ tell anyone. (not / tell)
quiz.explain: The negative of will is will not, contracted to won't. Promises are the natural home of will.

quiz.prompt: I think the meeting _____ longer than an hour. (last)
quiz.hint: "I think" tells you which future this is.
quiz.explain: Opinion cues like I think take will, and modals are followed by the bare infinitive: will last, never will lasts.
Both will be and is going to be are heard, but a fixed future fact that nobody chose is the classic home of will.
Questions invert the modal: Will they publish? No do, no to, no -ing.

quiz.prompt: Careful with that shelf — it _____ fall.
quiz.explain: Visible evidence, seconds away: going to. Will here would sound like a distant prediction rather than a warning.

quiz.prompt: I've decided. I _____ apply for the transfer.
quiz.explain: The decision was made before you spoke, so it takes going to. Will would contradict "I've decided".

quiz.prompt: The lid _____ come off. I've tried three times. (not / come)
quiz.hint: A refusal — even from an object.
quiz.explain: Won't expresses refusal, and English extends that to things that will not cooperate: the lid won't come off.

quiz.prompt: Call me when you _____ at the station. (arrive)
quiz.explain: After when, if, as soon as and until we use the present, even about the future: when you arrive, not when you will arrive.

quiz.prompt: If it rains tomorrow, we _____ the match. (cancel)
quiz.hint: First conditional — which half takes will?
quiz.explain: In a first conditional the if-half stays present and the result half takes will: If it rains, we will cancel.

quiz.prompt: Don't worry about the washing up — I _____ it later.
quiz.hint: An offer made on the spot.
quiz.explain: An offer decided as you speak: I'll do it. "I'm doing it" would mean it was already arranged.

quiz.prompt: By 2050 most new cars _____ electric, experts say.
quiz.explain: A distant prediction with no visible evidence takes will + bare infinitive: will be.

quiz.prompt: He _____ listen to anyone about it. (not / listen)
quiz.hint: Refusal again — about a person this time.
quiz.explain: Won't listen means refuses to listen. It is stronger and more personal than "doesn't listen".

results: Clean run. You can tell a decision from a plan, and a belief from a forecast.
Solid progress. Worth a look back at camp five before camp eight.
Good first attempt. The will/going to fork is the part to read again.
